No one has ever attempted the complete reconstruction of a crash of this magnitude. Drawing on interviews with hundreds of survivors, crew, and airport and rescue personnel, Laurence Gonzales, a commercial pilot himself, captures, minute by minute, the harrowing journey of pilots flying a plane with no controls and flight attendants keeping their calm in the face of certain death. He plumbs the hearts and minds of passengers as they pray, bargain with God, plot their strategies for survival, and sacrifice themselves to save others.

Laurence Gonzales is the son of a Mexican biophysicist and an Irish-German woman with a flair for poetry.

...

His career took off when he switched from poetry and fiction to nonfiction. As early as 1973, he had decided to bring together the worlds of science and poetry to create a new kind of nonfiction.

...

rs of research and experimentation, he brought those elements together in Deep Survival: Who Lives, Who Dies, and Why . That book created a genre, much imitated, and has remained a consistent best seller since its publication in 2003. Along the way, his unique style of journalism won him many awards, including two National Magazine Awards and the Montaigne Medal. Another achievement in his pursuit of this new approach to factual writing was Flight 232: A Story of Disaster and Survival . The first complete reconstruction of the fatal crash of a modern airliner, it was called "A kind of miracle" by Michael Korda and "a new masterpiece" by Richard Rhodes. It represented a landmark in journalism, penetrating an unseen and deadly realm of our daily lives, never before revealed, to demonstrate the beating heart of human compassion within. His most recent novel is Lucy. His most recent nonfiction book is Isolato: An Intimate Portrait of Cormac McCarthy

About the book
In **Flight 232**, Laurence Gonzales delivers a gripping
retelling of one of aviation's most harrowing disasters. As
United Airlines Flight 232 crashes near Sioux City, witnesses
observe a terrifying fireball, leading rescuers to believe no one
could survive the wreckage. Against all odds, 184 of the 296
passengers emerge alive from the chaos. Through extensive
interviews with survivors, crew, and first responders,
Gonzales—a seasoned commercial pilot—vividly recounts the
desperate struggle for survival amid catastrophic failure. He
explores the emotional resilience of the passengers, who
engage in prayers, bargaining, and self-sacrifice, while also
delving into the meticulous scientific investigations that
uncover a critical design flaw. **Flight 232** stands as a
powerful testament to human courage and ingenuity in the face
of tragedy, securing its place among the greatest aviation
narratives ever penned.
